vocab.title: Match each word to its meaning
defs: a long narrow passage between the shelves in a shop
another supply of the same medicine you were already prescribed
the part of the price the patient pays when insurance covers the rest
to use all of something, so that none is left
a written order from a doctor for a medicine
the printed information stuck to a medicine package
how much of a medicine to take, and how often
sold under its chemical name, without a brand

paras: ACTIVE INGREDIENT. Hydrocortisone 1%. PURPOSE: anti-itch. USES: for the temporary relief of itching associated with minor skin irritations, insect bites and rashes.

WARNINGS. For external use only. Do not use on broken skin, on the face, or in the eyes. Ask a doctor before use if you have a skin infection. When using this product, avoid contact with the eyes. Stop use and ask a doctor if the condition worsens, if symptoms last more than seven days, or if they clear up and return within a few days. Keep out of reach of children. If swallowed, get medical help or contact a poison control center right away.

DIRECTIONS. Adults and children two years of age and older: apply a thin layer to the affected area not more than three to four times daily. Children under two years: do not use, ask a doctor. You do not have to cover the area with a bandage. Wash your hands after each application.

OTHER INFORMATION. Store at room temperature. Do not use after the expiration date printed on the tube. INACTIVE INGREDIENTS: cetyl alcohol, glycerin, purified water, white petrolatum. QUESTIONS? Call the pharmacist at the number on the box, or 1-800 CARE, Monday to Friday, nine to five.
reading.source: Teaching label written for this lesson in the fixed Drug Facts format required on American over-the-counter packaging. The headings and the modal language are the target; the product is not a real brand and the text must not be used as a source of clinical information.

reading.prompt: What is the main idea of this label?
choices: This cream cures skin infections and can be used anywhere on the body.
It relieves itching for a short time, it has clear limits on where and how long to use it, and it tells you when to stop and ask a doctor.
It is a prescription medicine that only a pharmacist can hand over.

bank.label: Say it naturally
items: Excuse me, could you tell me which aisle this is in?
Is this safe with the tablet I already take?
Do you have the generic instead?
You must not use it on broken skin.
You should stop if the skin becomes more irritated.
You do not have to cover it with a bandage.

listenings.text: There are three things I say twenty times a day, and I would put them on a sign if they let me. The first one is the question almost nobody asks. People bring me something from the shelf and they ask what it does, which is on the box, and they do not ask whether it is safe with what they already take, which is not on the box. Half the problems I catch in a week are interactions with a tablet the customer did not think to mention, because in their head that tablet is not a medicine any more, it is just something they take. The second one is the generic. It is the same active ingredient, at the same dose, and very often it costs a fraction of what the brand costs. You do not need permission and you do not need to explain yourself. You can simply ask, is there a generic, and in most cases there is. And the third one is what to do when you run out of something on a Saturday night, which is when it always happens. Do not call the clinic. Call us. In most states we can give you an emergency supply for a few days while your prescriber is unavailable, and people go the whole weekend without their medication because nobody ever told them that.

The first thing that surprised me was that almost everything was just there, on an open shelf, in an aisle, and nobody was going to hand it to me. Where I come from you ask a person behind a counter and they bring it to you. Here you walk. And the aisles have numbers and signs, and I did not know the words on the signs, so I walked past what I needed four times. The first time I collected a prescription it went badly. They told me a price and I thought that was the price of the medicine, and it seemed impossible, so I argued with a very patient young man for about ten minutes. It was the copay. The insurance was paying the rest and nobody had explained the word to me, not once, in six months of paperwork. Now I have one sentence that I use every single time, and it embarrasses me how long it took me to learn it. Excuse me, could you tell me which aisle this is in? Four words, more or less, and they solved a year of walking in circles.

extra_audio.text: Excuse me, could you tell me which aisle this is in? I am here to pick up a refill. Is this safe with the tablet I already take? Do you have the generic instead? How much is the copay? I ran out of it on Sunday. What should I do?
